questions.q: What happens to unpromoted work in a sandbox when it's refreshed?
options: It is automatically merged into the new copy
It is overwritten and lost -- a refresh replaces the sandbox's contents with a fresh copy from its source
It is automatically backed up to production before the refresh runs
Refreshing has no effect on anything already inside the sandbox
questions.explain: A refresh is destructive to anything not yet promoted out -- a half-finished Flow, unsaved test data, or an undeployed change is gone once the fresh copy overwrites it.

questions.q: What is the minimum refresh interval for a Full sandbox?
options: 1 day
5 days
15 days
29 days
questions.explain: Salesforce enforces a 29-day minimum refresh interval for Full sandboxes, reflecting the much larger amount of data a Full sandbox copies compared to the other types.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a personal development sandbox usually should NOT be refreshed casually, even though Developer sandboxes can refresh daily?
options: Because Developer sandboxes are technically incapable of being refreshed
Because Developer sandboxes automatically refresh themselves every 24 hours regardless of user action
Because refreshing it risks wiping active, unpromoted work for no real benefit, since this tier doesn't depend on data freshness
Because refreshing a Developer sandbox requires written approval from Salesforce Support
questions.explain: The development tier is about speed and isolation, not data freshness -- a casual refresh there mostly just risks destroying someone's in-progress work for little gain.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend refreshing a staging sandbox close to a release window and ahead of each seasonal Salesforce release?
options: So that what's being tested reflects production as it currently is, including anything that changed since the last refresh, and so the upcoming platform release can be validated against current configuration
Because Salesforce requires a refresh before every release by policy, with no exceptions
Because refreshing close to a release window makes the refresh complete faster
Because seasonal releases automatically trigger a sandbox refresh with no action needed
questions.explain: Refreshing too rarely lets testing and staging drift away from what production actually looks like, quietly undermining the confidence a passed test was supposed to provide -- timing a refresh near the release window and the seasonal release keeps that confidence real.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what should happen before a sandbox is refreshed, given that a refresh is destructive?
options: The sandbox should be deleted first, then refreshed
All users should be removed from the sandbox permanently
Nothing -- refreshes can happen at any time without any check
Someone with clear ownership of the refresh calendar should confirm nothing valuable and unpromoted still lives only in that sandbox, and communicate the refresh in advance
questions.explain: Because a refresh wipes unpromoted work, a healthy strategy assigns clear ownership of the refresh calendar and checks in advance that nothing important exists only in that one sandbox.
